title: Part 2
text: shadow loomed cold across his mind, displeasure radiating from the Fog itself. Performance: unsatisfactory. Quota: unfulfilled. No excuses. The leash tightened. And the predator felt the cage closing in. Chapter 5: Fault Lines The campfire burned steady, sparks drifting upward into the endless dark, fading against the faint silhouettes of the treetops. Survivors lingered in wary silence, jittery in the aftermath of something they didn’t fully understand. The tension of the last match hadn’t fully left their muscles; the regular flow of the trial having been so dramatically altered from what they had come to expect that nobody was quite sure how to fully let it go. Dwight sat near the edge of the circle, spine too straight, hands tight on his knees. He wasn’t trembling, exactly, but his body hadn’t decided if it was entirely safe to uncoil yet. His breath came short, shallow. His glasses reflected the flames in little red glints that flickered and danced. He hadn’t said a word since they got back. Not until Jake broke the silence. “Are you gonna tell us what happened,” he asked, more edge than joke, “or just sit there like you saw the devil? You look like he damn near ripped you in half back there.” His tone was half-amused, but the tension betrayed him. Sure, Dwight had more anxiety than most of them, but none of them had seen him look quite like that before — pale, wide-eyed, barely able to stand after the trial ended. Dwight swallowed. His voice was quiet. “He had me.” “Wesker?” Feng asked, eyebrow raised. “So what? He always has you.” “No,” Dwight said quickly. “No, not like that. He had me— lifted. One hand. Slammed me into the wall, and then...” He hesitated, frowning against the memory, trying to find the words. His fingers flexed once, then clenched again. “Something stopped him. I don’t know how else to explain it. It was just us, and he completely had me, and then he just... let go. Not on purpose. It was like something hit him. Hard.” A silence fell over the fire. Jake exhaled slowly, arms crossed. “That... doesn’t sound like him.” “He’s been off,” Claudette murmured, almost to herself. “The last few matches. I thought it was just an off day or something, but... his swings are weird. Delayed. Off-balance.” “I thought I was imagining it,” Feng added. “But when I looped him by the greenhouse, he full- on missed a corner he never misses. Like, by a mile.” Jake grinned faintly. “Sounds like a win to me.” But his smile didn’t reach his eyes. None of theirs did. Something in them knew it wasn’t just sloppiness. Not really. Dwight’s knuckles whitened. “There’s something on his wrist. I saw it when he grabbed me. A band. Black, with these little red lights. It was glowing — sparking — when he dropped me. And his face...” He stopped again. Claudette turned toward him, tone soft. “What about it?” Dwight shook his head slowly, like the image still lingered somewhere behind his eyes. “It didn’t look like him. It looked —” He didn’t finish. He didn’t have to. The word hung in the air anyway, unspoken but understood. Human. The fire cracked, a log splitting with a sharp pop. “Well,” Meg said finally, arms folded tight across her chest, “regardless of what’s going on... it’s not our problem.” That earned her a few sideways glances, but she barreled forward. “I’m just saying. If something’s wrong with him — whatever that means — then that’s good news for us. We might actually survive a match without getting punched through a generator. I’m not gonna cry over it.” “It’s not about that,” Claudette said, her voice uneasy, “I don’t think it’s that simple.” “It kind of is,” Jake muttered. Dwight looked thoughtful for a moment. His fingers drummed once on his knee and stopped. His eyes stayed locked on the fire. “It felt like...” he started, then trailed off. He couldn’t explain the feeling in his chest when Wesker dropped him. Not fear. Not relief. Something worse. The afterimage of being gripped by something so powerful it could’ve crushed him without thought — and then realizing it tried and still couldn’t. That moment of recoil. The mask slipping. The confusion. The pain. And still, the man had looked him in the eye like a feral thing in a trap. Like it wasn’t just about failing to kill — it was about losing the choice. Dwight shivered. Claudette glanced sideways, picking nervously at the hem of her sleeve. “Do you think someone’s doing it on purpose?” “To him?” Jake frowned. “Why not?” she asked. “They mess with us all the time. Maybe someone is trying to balance the playing field.” “Sounds like they’re doing us a solid,” Meg muttered. Silence crept in again, stretching thin and uneasy. Across the Fog, beneath flickering fluorescents and old concrete, Wesker sat alone in the RPD’s western hallway. One elbow braced on his knee, wrist resting loosely in his other hand. The cuff hummed. Not loudly — not anymore. It didn’t have to. It pulsed like a second heart now, a low throb beneath skin and bone, threading into every twitch of seared, aching muscle. He knew they were talking about him. Didn’t need to hear the words. The Fog carried more than blood and footsteps. It carried intent. And something in the firelight across the way was pricking at him like needles behind the eyes. They thought he was slipping. They thought he was weak. And somewhere, just beneath the wires — behind the intercom crackle and rustling vents — came the faintest wheeze of laughter, as if Herman could hear it too. Chapter 6 - Judgement The next trial began with the usual surge of anticipation — Wesker stepped forward into the harsh sunlight of Coldwind, Uroboros stirring beneath his skin like a tide ready to break. He welcomed the power, clung to it. It was the last thread of certainty left to him. A sharp burning sensation stabbed against the back of his neck, but he rolled his shoulders against it, shaking it off. He had a quota to fill. Herman’s little toy was not getting in his way today. He reached for Uroboros, to bolster his speed and clear the area faster. The sooner he found the survivors, the sooner he could take them down and get back to the station. He felt the lift of energy, and without warning, the burning returned at the back of his neck, and the power was simply gone. The virus stilled. No writhing beneath the veins, no familiar burn gathering in his muscles. His healing edge dulled and vanished. His body felt heavier, slower. For the first time in years, he felt only human. He froze mid-stride, disbelief flashing sharp enough to cut. He tried again, reaching inward, demanding Uroboros answer. Nothing. Only the faint, mocking hum of the cuff at his wrist. The survivors noticed quickly. Ace darted across his vision, vaulting clean over a pallet. Wesker followed — slower, clumsier. When he reached for Uroboros to close the gap, his body refused. Wesker’s swing landed late, his knife bouncing off the wood, and Ace slipped free, laughing as he went. Nearby, Jake hesitated before bolting off a generator, his eyes flicking back in confusion. Uncertainty etched across his face, as if he had just seen a god limping across the cornfield; but even he eventually joined in on the easy run. Meg launched herself into the nearby shack and out of reach of his knife. He tried vaulting after her, legs refusing to align right mid-air, catching hard on the frame. Pain bloomed in his ribs as he hit the ground awkwardly. A window he once cleared with ease — now an obstacle. The Entity’s presence pressed heavy in his skull, cold and merciless, the spot on his neck flaring with heat. He reached back and felt at it, tracing the raised edges of a shape like a brand that had appeared out of nowhere. A set of jagged marks in small circle with a line. The Entity’s power limiter. He understood at once. This was punishment. Results had fallen. Quota unmet. She didn’t need to speak. Her judgment seeped from the soil, burned in the light, echoed in every missed strike. She was the Fog. The trial. The world. And she had deemed him insufficient. Earn them back, the whisper seemed to curl through the Fog. Prove your worth. Wesker’s teeth ground hard enough to ache. To be sabotaged by Herman was intolerable. But to be stripped bare by the Entity herself — reduced, grounded like a wayward child — was a degradation beyond measure. He forced himself onward, each step a weight. His fists still struck with brutal strength, but it was not the same. Every hook was slower. Every chase longer. The laughter of survivors rang sharper, crueler. They weren’t just surviving. They were enjoying it. And somewhere, Herman watched the data roll in, scribbling notes with delight as the great predator was left to flail as nothing more than flesh and bone. It didn’t take long for the difference to cut deep. Wesker still moved faster than any human had the right to. He still hit harder, his body honed by years of merciless conditioning. But without Uroboros threading his veins, his rhythm faltered. Every vault was mistimed, every chase a second too long. His instincts screamed to strike, to surge forward with inhuman speed — but his limbs betrayed him, sluggish and dull. Every second dragged with the weight of a body that no longer obeyed. The survivors capitalized on the situation. Pallets slammed into his shoulders, blast mines seared his vision, vaults taunted him just out of reach. He should have been untouchable, a storm breaking across the map. Instead, he felt like a blunt instrument swung too late. The cuff was infinitely worse now. Built for a monster, it tore straight through a man. Each shock locked his muscles longer; each jolt scrambled his vision harder. Chemical injections lingered in his system, refusing to flush out. His breath hitched in sharp coughs, his chest spasmed in arrhythmic bursts, sweat stinging his eyes as the toxins dragged him down. By mid-trial he was bleeding from pallet splinters and generator traps, staggering where once he would have walked unmarked. Hooks came harder, slower. The laughter of survivors at the exit gate carried like knives. He clenched his fists, refusing to yield, even as his knees trembled beneath him. Pride alone kept him moving, a stubborn refusal to collapse. But each pulse of the cuff reminded him — without Uroboros, without his healing, without his edge — he would just bleed out like any other man. And Herman’s notes would be exquisite. The Fog reclaimed its pieces when the trial ended. Survivors were carried back to the fire, laughing and shaken, while Wesker retreated into the station’s darkened corners. Normally the cycle reset him whole. Bruises gone, cuts erased, breath restored. Not this time. The cuff’s bite carried over. His chest still spasmed with every uneven beat, lungs dragging against phantom smoke from trapped generators. His vision twitched in static bursts, a faint afterimage of the Fog’s glare lingering at the corners of his eyes. The chemicals burned in his veins, heavier now that his body couldn’t purge them quickly. He fought the instinct to retch against it. It wouldn’t help, that much he could tell. For the first time in years, Wesker stayed broken between trials. Overhead, Herman’s voice slid through the intercom, muffled by the scratch of a pen. “Subject 06-W, post-trial observation. Damage persisting beyond reset cycle. Viral regression absolute. Healing factor absent. Collateral injuries amplified.” A pause, and the click of a smile audible behind the speaker. “Entity tolerance noted. No intervention to preserve asset. Most enlightening.” Wesker coiled inward, fingers digging into the cuff until his nails split. His pride demanded fury, denial, retribution. But the tremors in his muscles betrayed him with every breath. Herman hummed faint approval, as if to himself. “Good. Carry it with you. That tremor? That’s just the beginning. You’ll feel it unravel. I’ll make sure of it.” Chapter 7 – Fractures The survivors gathered close to the fire, its glow a fragile shield against the endless dark. The Fog pressed close tonight — not enough to burn, but enough to feel. Like a wall just beyond the firelight, breathing with quiet intent. No one dared move too far from the circle. The scent of blood still clung to some of them, faint but sharp, as if the last trial hadn’t quite let go. Dwight’s words still clung in the air from the last report. A cuff. Sparks. Wesker faltering. Kate leaned forward, eyes glinting. “So what? We should be celebrating. His trials are easy now. We walk out breathing. That’s a win.” Her grin was sharp, but the tremor in her leg betrayed the leftover fear. Jake tossed a twig into the fire, leaning back with arms folded. “Finally, some balance. Guy was overpowered as hell. Maybe the Fog finally nerfed him.” “He still threw me over a generator,” Meg muttered. “And I’m not gonna pretend he didn’t enjoy it.” “Well, maybe now he limps while he does it,” Jake quipped, but the way his fingers picked at a fading bruise on his jaw betrayed the memory of a very recent hit. Claudette wrung her hands, gaze fixed on the flames. “You didn’t see him. He wasn’t just slower. He looked... sick. Like it’s killing him.” Meg scoffed, but her voice wavered. “He’s still the one throwing us on hooks. Don’t forget that. If he’s hurting, good. He deserves worse.” Nea’s voice slipped in, hesitant but firm. “Still doesn’t feel right. Whatever else he is... he’s stuck here just like us. All the killers are. If he’s breaking down, that’s not a win. That’s—” “—that’s one less monster breathing down our necks,” Jake cut in, sharp. “I’m not losing sleep over it.” The fire popped. Silence weighed heavy. Some sat straighter, pride in their eyes at the thought of easier trials. Others hunched lower, unsettled by the image of a killer reduced to almost nothing overnight. A line had clearly been drawn — pragmatists on one side, bleeding hearts on the other. Dwight sat quiet, shoulders tense. He had seen it up close. Wesker’s snarl, his hand at his throat, and the look in his eyes as that power was stripped away in an instant. He could still feel the glow of the cuff radiating heat against his skin, and the way Wesker’s hand had spasmed away from him. He didn’t speak again. He didn’t have to. The fracture was already spreading rampant through the camp. Arguments grew sharper with each return to the fire. Meg’s bravado turned scathing. Jake mocked anyone who dared suggest sympathy. Feng puffed herself up, boasting about how easy her escapes had become. Claudette pleaded for caution, voice thin but insistent. “You don’t understand — if something can control him, then what stops it from controlling the others? What if we’re next?” Her pleas only earned her contempt back. “You sound crazy,” Meg snapped. “It’s not our problem. Let it break him.” The camp fractured further. Survivors started refusing to share strategies. Old habits died first — item swaps, generator routes, killer callouts. In one trial, Elodie lay slumped by a hook near the Asylum gates, bleeding out and begging quietly for help. Feng vaulted past without so much as a glance. “Should’ve picked a side,” she muttered. In another, Nea staggered toward Meg with a medkit outstretched, only to be waved off and left behind. The compassionate ones were ostracized, left whispering to each other in smaller clusters, tension thick as the firelight flickered across their faces. No one looked each other in the eye anymore. Through it all, Gabriel sat silent, his dark eyes thoughtful as the arguments flew. Dwight’s earlier insistence about the black band had set off something in his mind that he couldn’t quite let go. When some of the more antagonistic survivors had been taken by the Fog for trials, Gabriel took the opportunity to join Dwight at the fire. “Describe it to me. The cuff.” Dwight blinked at him. “What?” “You said it was seamless. Sparking. Fused to his skin. Tell me everything you saw.” Dwight swallowed, then recounted the details — the red glow, the sparks, the way Wesker clutched at it as if trying to tear it off. Claudette added her own memory of his faltering swings. Nea mentioned the way he staggered between hits. Gabriel’s frown deepened with every word. “It sounds almost like some kind of conductor. I doubt it’s actually seamless, it had to be applied to him somehow, but it sounds like it’s been screwing up his attacks for a while now,” he nodded, thoughtfully. His voice was calm, but the words carried weight. “If it’s actively controlling him, and that’s a huge IF, then it’s a risk to all of us. Rules are the only thing that let us survive in here. If something can break those rules, it’s not just his problem. It’s ours.” Uneasy silence followed. Even some of the pragmatists looked shaken, murmuring amongst each other with significantly less confidence than they had earlier. Gabriel rose slowly, dusting ash from his hands. “That settles it then. I need to see it myself. Up close.” He wasn’t foolish — getting close to a killer was a death sentence more often than not. But the real threat wasn’t Wesker’s claws. It was the silence from the Entity. The rules didn’t bend. They weren’t supposed to bend. “Are you sure about this?” Claudette followed him across the camp, clearly concerned. People didn’t just go actively hunting for the killers. “I don’t care what it takes,” Gabriel replied quietly. “I need to know if it’s the cuff that’s damaging him... or something worse. We can’t afford to not be sure about this. If something is changing, we need to be prepared for it.” Claudette hesitated, then touched his arm, voice dropping away from prying ears. “Just... be careful, ok? Whatever this is... I don’t think it’s done yet.” Chapter 8 – Too Close for Comfort The Fog dragged them in silent, heavy. The trial grounds felt close today, the tight corridors of Hawkins too near, the light too dim. Wesker moved quickly, boots cracking glass beneath him as he stepped into a shadowed hallway. He needed to find the survivors before Herman decided to destroy his quota yet again. The cuff at his wrist didn’t spark today, just low hum against his skin like a warning, a quiet reminder of the threat against him. Still, he moved better than the last trial. He had spent time getting used to moving around without the aid of the virus for the first time in ages, and though he was still sluggish and the coordination had yet to balance back out, he felt more confident in his steps. The Entity could have done far worse than suppress Uroboros on him. He had seen what She did to some of the other killers when they displeased Her. In comparison, this was practically a mercy. He wouldn’t waste it. He wouldn’t be humiliated again. He found the first one crouched near a generator. Claudette. She flinched when he stepped into view but didn’t run. Not right away. She looked up at him. Not with fear. With focus. Her gaze flicked to his wrist, held for half a heartbeat too long, then up to his face. Calculating. Quiet. Like she was cataloging something. She darted left and he followed, faster than he had in days. The chase should have felt good, but each footfall jolted aches and burns that wouldn’t heal, and his prey kept losing her focus on fleeing. Her eyes had already moved on. Not to the door. Not to safety. To the cuff. By the time he cornered her, someone else was watching. Nea this time, crouched on a ledge above. No flashlight. No attempt to save. Just eyes. She didn’t even flinch when he hooked Claudette. Wesker caught her gaze, the first sharp spark of unease rippling through him, before dipping back into the hallway. The second came when Gabriel tried to dodge a hit — too early. Wesker grabbed him instead, slamming him against a crate. He saw the man’s hand move reflexively to grip at his wrist, not to pull his grip away but instead to grab at the glowing band. He threw Gabriel off hard. Harder than he needed to. The cuff pulsed once in warning, then fell quiet. What was this? They were everywhere. Elodie baited a chase and never dropped her pallet. Nea looped him in tight circles that gave her no advantage. Gabriel cut close angles, always watching. No gens popped. No real escapes. They weren’t playing to win. They were playing to observe. Wesker struck Elodie down mid-vault, just to make it stop. Her scream was real. So was the blood. But even she looked up at him with that same damned expression. Not fear. Not hatred. Curiosity. He hooked her. And left her there for the Entity to claim. The Fog pressed close, pleased in the back of his skull, but it didn’t matter. He was being studied. Not like a weapon. Not like a god. Like a specimen. He lashed out. Windows shattered. Walls cracked. His stride turned savage, all rhythm gone. The survivors scattered, finally remembering to fear him. And yet even in flight, their heads turned. Eyes flicked to the cuff. He caught Nea once — barely. She slipped the grapple with a blast mine to the face. His vision swam. A second spark pulsed red-hot through the band. His knees nearly gave. He snarled and launched himself after her, only to catch sight of Gabriel again — standing too close. Waiting. A mistake soon corrected; his pained screams delivered to the Entity with considerably more vitriol than was appropriate. By the time the final generator roared to life, two hooks had been filled and the trial grounds looked clawed through. Blood on the tiles. Scrapes in the walls. Several heavy crates cracked in the corner. And Wesker? He stood in the center of it all, breath ragged, fist trembling at his side. His coat hung heavy with blood and sweat, eyes ringed with static flashes. The cuff was quiet. But he could feel it. The station lights flickered faintly. Wesker gripped the edges of the shower room sink, riding out a wave of pain and nausea. A hum crackled through the intercom. “Subject 06-W: survivor response escalating. Notable breakdown of cooperation. Factions forming. Efficiency decline evident.” A pause, and the scratch of his pen on paper. “Collateral observation: select survivors displaying heightened interest in monitoring equipment. Engineer among them. Pattern of curiosity spreading.” “Unintended consequence. Subjects developing interest in apparatus. Will require... mitigation.” A chuckle, low and pleased. “Can’t have the lab rats chewing through the wires.” The intercom clicked silent, leaving Wesker seething in his corner, cuff humming steadily. Chapter 9 – Malfunction The Fog belched them into rust and ruin — a shattered foundry wrapped in chains and crumbling metal. Wesker hit the ground running. For a heartbeat, he looked like himself; focused, powerful, hunting. Mid stride, his body seized, snapping sideways, his momentum pitching him off-balance as the cuff flared hotter than before. He slammed shoulder-first into stone, the impact jolting dust loose in a choking cloud. The roar he let out was guttural, shredded at the edges, humiliation bleeding into rage. From then on, the trial collapsed into chaos. There was no rhythm, no strategy, no grace. Just jagged surges and violent rebounds as Wesker tried to make his body obey. Muscles fired too late or too violently. One moment he hurled Steve into a wall with such force that plaster cracked outward in a spiderweb. The next, his knife struck a deep gouge into scenery instead of survivors — every mistimed impact punished with a jolt from the cuff that lit up the room. Sparks spat from the device with every failure, stinging the air with ozone. The world reeked of metal and heat and something burning beneath the skin. Inside his head, the betrayal was worse than the pain. His body had never refused him before, not since he carved himself into something more than human. Now every strike mocked him. He could feel their eyes watching, registering each misfire. Prey saw his weakness. He would rather have died on the spot than endure it. The survivors, though, didn’t see weakness. They saw something worse. An apex predator had rhythm: chase, lunge, recover. Predictable in its terror. But this? This was coin-flip chaos. Every time he rounded a corner, they didn’t know if he’d miss them entirely or strike so hard their bones would powder. Claudette pressed flat against a pallet, tears leaking silent as she watched the red flare at his wrist. Nea crept around a corridor edge, hood half off, staring at the sparks instead of his eyes. Gabriel crouched low near a half-finished gen, studying the erratic stutter of Wesker’s movements. They didn’t seem so random now that he was watching closely. They couldn’t look away. And they couldn’t linger. Because Wesker’s thrashing was still deadly, every jolt turning him more into a thrashing weapon. Pallets shattered under blows meant for flesh, walls cracked from impacts that should have been clean grapples. Metal walls dented where his fists drove too far. His voice was a storm, every snarl bouncing down the halls like a wild animal caught in a cage too small. There was no rhythm to dodge, no pattern to learn. Just violence, jagged and wrong. The survivors couldn’t get close — every angle dissolved into chaos before they could lock their eyes on what they needed. They fled because to stand too near was to risk being crushed by sheer chaotic force. They weren’t running from Wesker. They were running from a bomb. By the time the final gen sparked alive, the trial looked like a war zone. Steve limped through a hole in the wall that hadn’t existed when the match began. Nea had a cut on her forehead from a ricocheted board. Claudette’s fingers trembled as she reset a bandage that had soaked through mid-match. Gabriel hadn’t touched a gen. He spent the whole match watching, dodging, calculating, and still came back with a split eyebrow and a gouged side. At the gate, no one spoke. They didn’t need to. Even Gabriel looked shaken. Back at the fire, the warmth barely reached them. Claudette sat closest, her arms wrapped tight around herself. “Those sparks...” Her voice cracked. “They weren’t random. Every time he froze, every time he twitched, it lit up.” Nea shoved her hood back, hair sticking damp to her temple. “And the sound. You heard it, right? Like something shorting out. Circuits frying. I’ve built enough rigs to know.” Jake barked a laugh, but it was hollow. “So what? He’s frying alive, big deal. Easier for us.” But he wouldn’t meet anyone’s eyes. “That’s not the point, Jake!” Claudette snapped, sharper than usual. “It’s not some coincidence he’s losing trials! That band is clearly driving him insane.” Meg laughed — too loud. “Oh, come on. A conspiracy now? What, he’s got a car battery under his coat for the sparking effect? He’s just slipping. End of story.” But her bravado cracked as her voice pitched too high. She looked away, jaw clenched. Gabriel settled onto a log, fresh wrappings over his side already seeping through. He rested his elbows on his knees, eyes on the fire. His voice was calm. Measured. “I couldn’t get close enough to really see,” he said. “But it’s definitely hardware. And if it’s hardware...” He lifted his gaze, scanning the circle. “...then someone’s using it.” The fire popped. No one laughed. No one argued. Even the pragmatists shifted, restless. The image of Wesker tearing through the trial like a cornered animal — sparks flying, screams echoing, walls coming down around him — clung to them all. The Fog hadn’t just unbalanced him. It had weaponized his suffering. Later, when the others had drifted into uneasy silence or disappeared into the tents, Gabriel stayed by the fire — gaze distant, mind still racing. He hadn’t seen it close enough. How was it situated? Could he get it off? He needed a closer look, but there was only one way to get it. Next time... he’d let Wesker grab him. Not for long. Just long enough. He had to know. Chapter 10 – Residue The reset came, but it didn’t bring peace. Wesker dropped to the floor of the station like a severed cable, his body refusing to respond with anything resembling precision. For a moment he stayed there — not by choice, but because his limbs simply wouldn't move. He tried to rise. Failed the first time. Vision swam. His stomach lurched. Knees crumpled. A palm caught the wall — and left a smear of red where it dragged down the paneling. That shouldn't still be there. The Fog was supposed to take these things — blood, sweat, breath. Pain. That was the contract. The pattern. The law. But lately... the Fog was leaving things behind. His body still heaved with the last trial’s ruin. Every breath dragged as if through smoke. His chest spasmed mid-inhale, ribs jerking under phantom pressure. Something hot clung to his spine like oil. His fingers trembled. Muscles flinched from old burns that should’ve never made it past the gate. The cuff at his wrist didn’t hum. Didn’t burn. Just sat there — quiet now. Patient. He gently prodded at the limiter mark on his neck and found the raised lines
